title: [RFC]: Add a configurable MoE feed-forward layer to DFlash2
body:
## Motivation

DFlash2 currently fixes every decoder layer to a dense Qwen3 MLP. A configurable routed-plus-shared MoE FFN allows sparse draft models while preserving DFlash2 attention, local convolutions, candidate selection, and block geometry.

## Proposed design

Add `draft_ffn_type: dense | moe` to DFlash2. The MoE option uses the Transformers Qwen3.5 routed/shared expert layout and serializes fused expert tensors directly in the checkpoint. The existing dense path remains the default and behaviorally unchanged.

Initial scope intentionally excludes expert parallelism, router auxiliary objectives, verifier-to-draft warm start, and serving-runtime changes. Those can be reviewed independently after the model contract is accepted.

## Validation

The prepared implementation includes config round-trip, dense-default compatibility, fused checkpoint key layout, fail-closed geometry, and reference MoE forward/backward tests. The branch is `qianlihuang:feat/dflash2-moe-ffn`.

title: [RFC]: Add a warmup-stable-decay learning-rate scheduler
body:
## Motivation

Drafter training often benefits from holding the peak learning rate for most of a run and concentrating annealing in a short final phase. The current trainer exposes linear and cosine schedules but cannot express warmup-stable-decay (WSD) without external patches.

## Proposed interface

Add `scheduler_type: wsd` with:

- configurable warmup initial LR ratio
- configurable final minimum LR ratio
- configurable final-decay fraction
- linear, cosine, exponential, and minus-square-root final-decay curves

All ratios scale each optimizer parameter group relative to its own peak LR, including the multi-optimizer Muon path. Invalid or overlapping phase geometry fails closed.

## Scope

This is an independent trainer feature. It does not change any draft-model architecture or add model-specific recipes. A focused implementation and scheduler tests are ready on `qianlihuang:feat/wsd-scheduler`.

title: [Feature request]: Support DFlash 2 drafters (path selector + local convolution)
body:
## Feature request: Support DFlash 2 drafters (path selector + local convolution)

### Summary
Speculators already supports the original DFlash training algorithm
(anchored-block drafting), but Inco AI's follow-up, **DFlash 2**
(https://inco.ai/blog/dflash2/, Aug 18 2026), adds two small modules on
top of the existing DFlash backbone that aren't currently supported:

1. **Lightweight pairwise path selector** — scores every adjacent pair of
   top-16 candidates per position and greedily/samples a coherent path
   through them, instead of taking each position's independent top-1 pick.
2. **Two-tap dynamic depthwise convolution** — inserted before/after each
   attention and MLP sublayer, mixing each draft position's hidden state
   with its predecessor's to reduce "suffix decay" toward the end of the
   block.

Both are cheap (~2M and ~16.5M added params respectively, <1.5% added
draft–verify cycle latency combined) and reportedly raise acceptance
length ~20%+ over plain DFlash.

Notably, Inco AI's own benchmarks show DFlash 2 outperforming DSpark drafters. 
On Qwen3.5-4B (per-request mean acceptance length):

| Dataset   | MTP  | DFlash | DSpark | DFlash 2 |
| --------- | ---- | ------ | ------ | -------- |
| GSM8K     | 4.78 | 4.99   | 5.69   | **6.20** |
| MATH-500  | 5.04 | 5.42   | 6.20   | **6.76** |
| HumanEval | 4.84 | 5.43   | 5.80   | **6.28** |
| MBPP      | 4.16 | 4.49   | 4.96   | **5.41** |
| MT-Bench  | 3.90 | 4.26   | 4.77   | **5.20** |
| Mean      | 4.54 | 4.92   | 5.49   | **5.97** |

### Motivation
Two DFlash 2 checkpoints are already public on Hugging Face:
- `incoai/Qwen3.8-27B-DFlash2`
- `incoai/Muse-Glimmer-30B-DFlash2`

and are runnable today via a fork/PR of SGLang, vLLM, and llama.cpp (see
the blog's "Run It Now" section). It'd be great to have first-class
support in Speculators so these (and future DFlash 2 drafters) can be
trained/converted/served through the standard Speculators → vLLM path,
consistent with existing DFlash support.

### Reference material
- DFlash 2 blog post: https://inco.ai/blog/dflash2/
- Original DFlash repo (architecture DFlash 2 builds on): https://github.com/z-lab/dflash/
- DFlash 2 checkpoints: https://huggingface.co/collections/incoai/dflash-2-6a8432273c9998ce1685d4c5

cc @jianc99 @xiziqiao @zhijian-liu

title: [RFC]: Add Medusa speculator (parallel decoding heads)
body:
### Motivation.

Speculators trains EAGLE-family, MTP, and DFlash drafters for vLLM but lacks Medusa, one of the most widely adopted speculative-decoding methods. Medusa (ICML 2024, [arXiv 2401.10774](https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.10774), `FasterDecoding/Medusa`) attaches K lightweight heads on the target's last hidden state to predict positions t+1..t+K in parallel. It runs natively in vLLM (`v1/spec_decode/medusa.py`, `{"method": "medusa"}`), TensorRT-LLM, and HF TGI.

Adding it lets users train Medusa heads here and deploy them straight to vLLM, and convert existing `FasterDecoding/Medusa` checkpoints.

### Proposed Change.

Add Medusa as a new speculator type. It has no draft transformer or recursive feedback, so it gets its own model/config rather than a flag:

1. **Model + config.** `MedusaDraftModel` / `MedusaSpeculatorConfig` (registered via `SpeculatorModel.register("medusa")` and `SpeculatorModelConfig.register("medusa")`): K residual MLP heads over the verifier's last hidden state, reusing `DraftVocabMixin` for the head vocab.
2. **Training.** Reuse the existing verifier-last-hidden-state pipeline (already extracted for eagle3/dflash); train heads with per-head loss against shifted targets (Medusa-1, frozen backbone).
3. **Converter.** Add a `MedusaConverter` for external `FasterDecoding/Medusa` checkpoints (remap head weights, build config from the verifier).
4. **vLLM parity.** Emit config compatible with vLLM's `{"method": "medusa"}` runtime so checkpoints deploy directly.

### Any Other Things.

Reference: Medusa, ICML 2024 — https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.10774

title: [RFC]:Train a Dense MLA DSpark draft for GLM-5.2 (DCP-compatible)
body: ### Motivation. ## Summary Add an optional **Dense MLA** decoder on DFlash / DSpark drafts (`--draft-arch glm5`) so the draft attention uses the same compressed KV page spec as the GLM-5.2 verifier (`kv_lora_rank + qk_rope_head_dim`). Serving can then keep **DCP (Decode Context Parallelism)** on for *both* the target and the drafter, instead of pairing an MLA verifier with a GQA draft. This is not a new speculative algorithm: the block-parallel mask, dual-source KV injection, Markov head, and confidence head stay the same. Only the attention implementation and the export contract change. After 1 epoch on 600k samples (single node), training loss converges. On GSM8K the served checkpoint reaches mean acceptance length **5.01 / 8** (`block_size = 8`). --- ## Motivation ### DCP is a first-class path for MLA targets, not an optional extra GLM-5.2 is a DeepSeek-style **MLA** verifier: K/V are compressed to `kv_lora_rank`, RoPE runs only on `qk_rope_head_dim`, and the engine stores KV as a **576-d page** (default `512 + 64`). DCP exists for that layout. [vllm#23734](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/23734) added Decode Context Parallel for MLA by interleaving those compressed pages across ranks inside the TP group — the point is to cut per-GPU KV memory on long context without growing world size. For a 753B-class GLM-5.2 verifier, that KV-capacity path is not optional: - Sparse MLA + DCP is what Hopper picks for GLM-5.2 / DeepSeek-V3.2 at modest per-rank head counts (e.g. TP4/DCP4 `fp8_ds_mla`); [vllm#46514](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/46514) is the work to stop that path from refusing DCP outright. - Measured on GLM-5.2-NVFP4, DCP=4 vs DCP=1 is ~**2.2×** GPU KV tokens (450k vs 205k) at the same TP — that is the reason to turn DCP on ([vllm#48392](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/48392)). Prefill Context Parallel (PCP) is the matching long-prefill story ([vllm#25749](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/25749)). Speculative decoding currently assumes the drafter inherits the target's parallel mapping, which is exactly where an MLA target + GQA draft falls over. ### An MLA verifier with a GQA draft is a known DCP incompatibility Default DFlash / DSpark drafts are **Qwen3 GQA**: independent `q_proj` / `k_proj` / `v_proj`, KV stored as `num_key_value_heads × head_dim`. Paired with GLM-5.2 that is three mismatches, not one: 1. **Page layout.** Verifier pages are `(kv_lora, k_rope)`. GQA draft pages are per-head K/V. DCP cannot apply one split/schedule rule to both graphs. 2. **Head-count semantics.** GQA synthesis sometimes rewrites `num_attention_heads` from `hidden_size / head_dim`. MLA compresses by LoRA rank; head count must follow the verifier. 3. **RoPE width.** GLM `rope_interleave=true` rotates adjacent pairs on `qk_rope_head_dim` only. GQA does NeoX split-half over the full `head_dim`. vLLM already documents this pairing as a problem, and the workarounds all tax the serving graph: | Upstream | What it shows | | --- | --- | | [vllm#53673](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/53673) (RFC, open) | Spec decode assumes the drafter uses the target's PCP/DCP mapping. Explicit example: **Kimi K3 (MLA, so DCP makes sense for the target) paired with a GQA draft** — “it probably makes sense to **disable DCP for the draft model**, since GQA already shards KV heads across TP and DCP would just add latency.” That is the GQA workaround: two parallel configs, draft off DCP. | | [vllm#48380](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/48380) (bug, open) | GLM-5.2 / DeepSeek-V3.2 with `--kv-cache-dtype fp8_ds_mla` + DSpark **fails to load**: the dense Qwen3-style draft inherits the target's MLA-only cache layout, which no dense backend accepts. The same report adds a fail-fast for DCP>1 because the draft slot mapping is DCP-blind and acceptance **silently collapses to ~0%**. | | [vllm#48392](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/48392) (PR, open) | Dense (GQA/MHA) DFlash/DSpark under DCP. Root cause, reported in the [vllm#46514](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/46514) discussion: the GLM-5.2 DSpark draft is MHA (64q/64kv); under TP4 each rank holds a 16-head shard, then DCP all-gathers 64 query heads and GQA-remaps them onto the **wrong** KV heads. Acceptance: DCP=1 **2.40** → DCP=4 **1.10** (collapse). The dense-path fix is to **replicate KV heads across the DCP group**. | | [vllm#52188](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/52188) | Complementary MLA draft + DCP path (Kimi-K3): **one latent KV head, no head-gather**. That is the shape that DCP was designed for. [vllm#48392](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/48392) states this explicitly: “#52188 enables the MLA draft path … this PR enables the dense path, where the head-gather is exactly what breaks.” | | [vllm#51705](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/51705) | ROCm Kimi-K3 DSpark + DCP: target MLA KV is DCP-sharded; the draft must use the **same DCP-local ownership** for metadata, block tables, and slots, or target and draft disagree about shard ownership and verification rows. | A GQA DSpark can train and serve with DCP **off**. Turn DCP **on** for GLM-5.2 and the dense draft is either unloadable ([vllm#48380](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/48380)), silently wrong ([vllm#46514](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/46514) / [vllm#48392](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/48392)), or forced off DCP while the 753B verifier stays on it ([vllm#53673](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/53673)). None of those keep one KV rule for the whole speculative graph. ### Why the verifier *and* the draft should both be MLA DCP (and PCP) shard **pages**, not “some attention module.” If the verifier page is `(kv_lora, k_rope)` and the draft page is per-head GQA, every later feature that walks those pages — DCP split, `fp8_ds_mla` quantization, slot mapping, CUDA-graph dummy runs, PD disagg — needs a second code path or a second parallel config. Training a Dense MLA draft (no DSA indexer) that matches the verifier's 576-d page means: 1. **One DCP split rule** for target and draft, the same reason Kimi-K3 MLA drafts work under DCP without head-gather ([vllm#52188](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/52188)). 2. **DCP stays on for the draft**, instead of the [vllm#53673](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/53673) default of disabling it for GQA drafters. Turning DCP off only on the draft still leaves two cache topologies and extra runner special cases; turning it off on the target throws away the KV-capacity win on GLM-5.2. 3. **No dense-path KV-head replication.** [vllm#48392](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/48392) is the correct serving patch *given* today's GQA checkpoint; it is not a substitute for training an isomorphic draft. Replication adds all-gather on K/V and still does not produce an MLA page. 4. **MLA-only cache dtypes can be shared instead of papered over.** [vllm#48380](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/48380) fails because a dense draft cannot consume `fp8_ds_mla`. An MLA draft can use the same compressed layout the verifier already selected. Keep DFlash dual-source KV and the block mask; swap only the attention implementation so the trained checkpoint is something DCP-aware serving can consume as `Glm5DSparkForCausalLM`. --- ## Alternatives considered | Option | Why not | | --- | --- | | Disable DCP on the GQA draft only / keep a non-MLA draft page ([vllm#53673](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/53673)) | DCP is the KV and throughput path on large MLA models. Draft-only DCP-off still splits the serving graph into two KV rules and is hard to maintain. | | Replicate GQA KV heads across the DCP group ([vllm#48392](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/48392)) | Fixes today's dense checkpoint; extra comm; still not the verifier's 576-d page; `fp8_ds_mla` still does not apply to the draft ([vllm#48380](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/48380)). | | New algorithm type (e.g. `glm5_dspark`) | The algorithm is still DSpark. Splitting a type would duplicate Markov / confidence / the train loop. `--draft-arch glm5` swaps the decoder. | | Use HF `glm5` config as the draft | `AutoConfig.for_model("glm5")` can resolve to HuggingFace's GLM config, not the local draft config. Always construct `Glm5Config`; promote `model_type` to `glm5_dspark`. | | Port the DSA indexer | GLM-5.2 verifiers may carry DSA; the draft is dense under the DFlash block mask. Indexer is out of scope. | --- ### Proposed Change. ## Proposed Change Swap MLA attention into the existing DFlash backbone; DSpark only changes the export class name. Training goes through `TrainConfig` — do not hard-code argparse fields in `scripts/train.py`. ```mermaid flowchart LR subgraph train [TrainConfig] draftArch["draft_arch glm5"] loraRank["q_lora_rank / kv_lora_rank"] end subgraph backbone [DFlash backbone] ctx["context_proj + context_norm"] rope["RoPE width = qk_rope_head_dim"] mla["Glm5DFlashMLAAttention"] end subgraph dspark [DSpark] markov[MarkovHead] conf[ConfidenceHead] export["architectures Glm5DSparkForCausalLM"] end draftArch --> mla loraRank --> mla ctx --> mla rope --> mla mla --> markov mla --> conf mla --> export ``` ### 1. Dense MLA layer New `src/speculators/models/dflash/glm5.py`: - `Glm5Config` (`model_type=glm5_dspark`), defaults lock the 576-d page: `kv_lora_rank=512`, `qk_rope_head_dim=64`. - Q comes only from draft hidden via Q-LoRA (`q_a` → RMSNorm → `q_b`); `q_lora_rank=0` falls back to a full `q_proj`. - K/V run `kv_a` on `cat(target_context, draft)` (`kv_lora_rank + qk_rope`) then `kv_b` (nope + V). - RoPE applies only on `qk_rope_head_dim`, interleaved pairs `(0,1), (2,3), ...`, matching `rope_interleave=true`. - GLM-5.2: `v_head_dim == qk_head_dim` (256). If `v != qk`, pad V for SDPA (defensive). `Qwen3DFlashDecoderLayer.attention_class` is factored out so `Glm5DFlashDecoderLayer` can override it. ### 2. DFlash wiring `dflash/core.py`: - `is_glm5_mla_config` → `Glm5DFlashDecoderLayer`, else Qwen3 GQA. - Rotary cache: `deepcopy` then `head_dim = qk_rope_head_dim`; do not mutate transformer config `head_dim`. - MLA export names: `context_proj` / `context_norm`. GQA keeps `fc` / `hidden_norm`. `_project_context()` covers both. - `_no_split_modules` includes `Glm5DFlashDecoderLayer`. `dflash/config.py`: `model_type in {glm5, glm5_dspark}` always builds `Glm5Config(**dict)` so `AutoConfig.for_model` cannot land on HF GLM. `--draft-config` uses the same mapping. ### 3. DSpark export contract vLLM-Ascend dispatches drafts by architecture name (K3 → `K3DSparkForCausalLM`). MLA drafts: - `DSparkSpeculatorConfig.architectures = ["Glm5DSparkForCausalLM"]` - `save_pretrained` restores that name after HuggingFace overwrites it with the Python class Forward / Markov / confidence head are unchanged. **Do not** `.detach()` the confidence head (unrelated to MLA; would change existing GQA DSpark backward). This repo owns training and the checkpoint contract. Loading `Glm5DSparkForCausalLM`, MLA causal / non-causal decode, and DSpark proposer integration are [vllm-ascend#14535](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm-ascend/pull/14535) (open at writing). Both sides agree on the export name so a trained checkpoint loads into that model class. ### 4. TrainConfig `DraftArgs` gains: - `draft_arch: Literal["llama", "qwen3", "glm5"] | None` - `q_lora_rank` / `kv_lora_rank` (optional overrides; `q_lora_rank=0` disables Q-LoRA) Validation: `glm5` is dflash / dspark only; LoRA rank overrides require `glm5` (or a glm5 `--draft-config`). `create_transformer_layer_config`: copy MLA dims from the verifier, **keep** verifier `num_attention_heads`, resolve RoPE width from `qk_rope_head_dim`. ### vs Qwen3 GQA | | Qwen3 GQA (default) | GLM-5 Dense MLA | | --- | --- | --- | | Flag | `--draft-arch qwen3` | `--draft-arch glm5` | | Q | `q_proj` + per-head RMSNorm | Q-LoRA (or full `q_proj`) | | K/V | independent `k_proj` / `v_proj` | `kv_a` + `kv_b`, compressed latent | | Dual-source KV | `cat(k_ctx, k_noise)` same proj | `kv_a(cat(target, draft))` | | RoPE | full `head_dim`, NeoX split-half | `qk_rope_head_dim` only, interleaved pairs | | Context proj | `fc` / `hidden_norm` | `context_proj` / `context_norm` | | Export `architectures` | `DSparkSpeculator` | `Glm5DSparkForCausalLM` | | DCP | conflicts with GLM-5.2 MLA pages ([vllm#53673](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/53673), [vllm#48392](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/48392), [vllm#48380](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/48380)) | same page spec as the verifier | --- ## Non-goals - No new speculative algorithm type; no change to DSpark loss or Markov training semantics. - No DSA indexer. - Do not merge cluster-address `train-glm52-*.sh` scripts. - Do not claim `glm5` as a supported generic vLLM CUDA draft. Ascend serving is [vllm-ascend#14535](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm-ascend/pull/14535), outside this RFC's code. --- ### Any Other Things. ## Experiments Run on `speculators-mla` with the same MLA draft as this RFC (sunny is a same-source port). Hyperparameters follow `train-glm52-1node.sh`; cluster addresses are not copied here. ### Setup | Item | Value | | --- | --- | | Verifier | GLM-5.2 | | Algorithm | DSpark, `--draft-arch glm5` | | Draft layers | 5, all full attention | | `block_size` | 8 | | Data | 600k rows, 1 epoch, `train-data-ratio=0.96` | | Parallel | 1 node, 16 NPU, `--fsdp-shard` | | Optim | `lr=5e-4`, cosine | | Sequence | `--total-seq-len 4096`, `--max-anchors 600` | | Loss | `{"ce": 0.1, "tv": 0.9}`, `--dflash-decay-gamma 10` | | Heads | `markov_rank=256`, confidence head on | | Attention | `--draft-attn-impl sdpa` | | Aux layers | `--target-layer-ids 2 22 38 58 74` | About **17 750** global steps. ### Training curves | Metric (EMA α=0.1, last step) | Value | | --- | --- | | `train/loss` | 0.924 | | `train/accept_rate` | 0.563 | | `train/accept_len` | 3.928 (in-block accept length from the train log; chart reference line 5.0) | ### GSM8K serving Same checkpoint, speculative decode on GSM8K (`block_size=8`): | Metric | Value | | --- | --- | | Average acceptance length | **5.01 / 8** | | Overall acceptance rate | 50.11% | | Total drafts / draft tokens / accepted tokens | 27 314 / 218 512 / 109 502 | | Output token throughput | 455.30 tok/s | | Total token throughput | 510.24 tok/s | | TPOT (excl. first token) mean / P50 | 25.46 ms / 23.30 ms | | TTFT mean / P50 | 2051.17 ms / 555.33 ms | Per-position accept rate (slots 0–7): | 0 | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 | 6 | 7 | | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | | 87.97% | 74.72% | 62.90% | 51.91% | 42.57% | 34.06% | 26.89% | 19.89% | End-of-block decay matches DSpark (block-parallel, position dependence weakens). Mean accept length ≈ 5 shows the MLA draft is usable on GLM-5.2, not only that train loss went down. [vllm-ascend#14535](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm-ascend/pull/14535) also reports a **GLM-5.2 W4A8 verifier + MLA DSpark BF16** GSM8K-subset preview (vLLM `v0.27.1`): `acceptance_len=4.59`, per-position rates about `[0.874, 0.729, 0.593, 0.479, 0.382, 0.301, 0.233]`. Not the same slice as the full GSM8K table (5.01 / 8), but the same order of magnitude — the training contract lines up with the Ascend serve path. --- ## Testing Unit tests: ```bash pytest tests/unit/models/test_glm5_dflash.py \ tests/unit/train/test_cli_args.py \ tests/unit/train/config/test_schema.py \ tests/unit/models/test_dflash_attention.py \ tests/unit/models/test_dspark_model_definitions.py ``` Coverage: interleaved RoPE pairs, MLA weight names (`q_a` / `kv_a` / `context_proj`), finite forward loss, config roundtrip (legacy `model_type=glm5` upgrades), `save_pretrained` exports `Glm5DSparkForCausalLM`, CLI/schema allow/deny for `glm5`. --- ## Drawbacks and limitations - **`--draft-arch glm5` is dflash / dspark only.** Eagle-3 / P-EAGLE / MTP still use llama / qwen3 / native layers. - **Train name vs serve name.** Training accepts `glm5`; on disk `model_type` is `glm5_dspark` and architecture is `Glm5DSparkForCausalLM`, loaded by [vllm-ascend#14535](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm-ascend/pull/14535). Generic vLLM CUDA draft serving is not claimed. - **No DSA.** The draft is dense under the DFlash mask; when the GLM-5.2 verifier has DSA, the indexer lives only on the verifier. - **1 epoch / 600k rows.** GSM8K accept length 5/8 is that data scale, not a ceiling. Longer training or domain data may lift late-block accept rates. - **TTFT tail.** GSM8K TTFT P99 is high; more likely serving batching / scheduling than the MLA draft itself. This RFC does not treat it as an architecture regression. --- ## References - DFlash: [arXiv:2602.06036](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.06036) - DSpark: [arXiv:2607.05147](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.05147) - DeepSeek-V2 MLA: [arXiv:2405.04434](https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.04434) - DCP for MLA: [vllm#23734](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/23734) - MLA target + GQA draft should disable DCP on the draft: [vllm#53673](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/53673) - Dense DSpark inherits MLA-only `fp8_ds_mla` / DCP-blind slots: [vllm#48380](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/48380), [vllm#48381](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/48381) - Dense GQA/MHA DFlash/DSpark under DCP (acceptance collapse): [vllm#48392](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/48392), report in [vllm#46514](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/46514) - MLA DSpark + DCP (Kimi-K3, no head-gather): [vllm#52188](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/52188), [vllm#51705](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/51705) - Serving adapter: [vllm-ascend#14535](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm-ascend/pull/14535) (`[Feature] Support GLM-5.2 MLA DSpark`, open) - Implementation: `src/speculators/models/dflash/glm5.py`, `dflash/core.py`, `dspark/config.py`, `dspark/core.py`, `src/speculators/train/config/schema.py`, `scripts/train.py`

title: [Bug]: test_eagle3_qwen3_8b_sharegpt fails acceptance threshold at token 0
body:
## Your current environment

- **vLLM** — `0.25.1`
- **Speculators** — `60cd983` (main, pre-release)
- **CUDA** — 13.0
- **PyTorch** — `2.12.1+cu130` test venv — **before** the `<=2.13.0` bump
- **Transformers** — `5.14.1`
- **Hardware** — 1× H100 80 GB, `ibm-wdc-k8s-h100-solo`
- **Model** — `Qwen/Qwen3-8B` (EAGLE-3, sharegpt)

## 🐛 Describe the bug

Sub-issue of #885.

`tests/e2e/regression/test_training_only_acceptance.py::test_eagle3_qwen3_8b_sharegpt` fails its acceptance assertion:

```
Acceptance 0.39957939011566773 at token 0 is less than threshold 0.4
```

Not a crash — an assertion on a trained model's quality metric. No CUDA fault, no OOM, no worker abort.

### Failing jobs

Both in run [`30138641585`](https://github.com/neuralmagic/llm-compressor-testing/actions/runs/30138641585) (2026-07-25):

| job | python | observed `acceptance_at_token_0` | threshold | shortfall |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| [`89627475848`](https://github.com/neuralmagic/llm-compressor-testing/actions/runs/30138641585/job/89627475848) | 3.10 | `0.39957939011566773` | `0.4` | **0.105 %** |
| [`89627475794`](https://github.com/neuralmagic/llm-compressor-testing/actions/runs/30138641585/job/89627475794) | 3.13 | `0.38689866939611056` | `0.4` | 3.3 % |

2 occurrences across the 4 archived runs that executed this test; both in the 07-25 run, none since.

### Not a torch 2.13 regression

Both occurrences are on torch `2.12.1+cu130`, **before** #869 raised the bound. Neither torch-`2.13.0` run reproduced it, and the test passed in every job of the v0.7.0 release run. Filed so the release-CI signal is accounted for in full, and flagged so it is not folded into the torch-2.13 work.

### Open questions

- `89627475848` missed by roughly one part in a thousand; `89627475794` by 3.3 %. These may not share one explanation — the first is consistent with threshold marginality, the second may indicate genuine variance in trained quality.
- Whether the underlying acceptance rate has drifted, or has always sat near `0.4` with the threshold set too tight. Needs the historical metric series, not pass/fail.
- The distribution of `acceptance_at_token_0` across repeated runs at fixed versions — no repeated-run data was collected.
- Whether the `[0.4, 0.1, 0.01]` thresholds were derived from a measured distribution or chosen as round numbers.

title: [RFC]: Add XPress training pipeline support
body:
### Motivation.


A block-diffusion drafter such as DFlash proposes a whole block of draft tokens in one forward pass, which makes drafting cheap. The cost is accuracy: the block is decoded from per-position marginals, so token *k* is drawn without seeing what the drafter chose at *k-1*. Nothing ties the positions together, while the target model verifies conditionally, so blocks that are individually plausible but jointly improbable get rejected early. That caps the achievable acceptance length.

We would like to contribute XPress, which restores the missing causality without a token-by-token loop, as a first-class speculator alongside DFlash and DSpark rather than as a fork. On Qwen3-8B it raises acceptance length over the Markov head on every benchmark we measured, at both temperatures, and over the plain DFlash drafter it is worth about +30% acceptance and ~1.3x end-to-end throughput on average. Full tables are in the third field.

Paper: xPress: Parallel Refinement for Diffusion Drafters in Speculative Decoding (https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02438).

### Proposed Change.


A new speculator, `xpress`, registered next to the existing ones.

**The refiner head.** Per position it reads the drafter's hidden state, a block-global summary and the previous token's embedding, fuses them into a low-rank space (r = 256), mixes across positions with a lower-triangular (causal) linear mixer, passes through an r-space SwiGLU MLP, and reads back out as a bias on the target LM head's logits. Everything except the two vocabulary projections lives in the bottleneck (~80M params, 96% of which are those two matrices). The whole refiner is:

```python
lat = self.token_embed(prev_token_ids)                    # [N, B, r]
x   = self.in_proj(torch.cat([hcache, lat], dim=-1))      # 3r -> r
l_eff = self.mix_l * self.causal_tril                     # lower-triangular, per channel
x = x + torch.einsum("ckj,njc->nkc", l_eff, x)            # causal mix across the block
x = x + self.mlp_down(F.silu(self.mlp_gate(x)) * self.mlp_up(x))
return self.readout(x)                                    # r -> V, a bias on the base logits
```

`hcache` is the pass-invariant `[down_h(h) ; down_g(g)]`, computed once per block and reused. `mix_l` is initialised to zeros, so at init the mixer is the identity and the head starts as a pure previous-token bias.

**Parallel refinement.** Because the mixer is causal, the block is resolved by Jacobi iteration rather than a left-to-right loop: the same call runs K times, each pass re-feeding the previous pass's argmax, so all positions update at once and the serial depth is K (a small constant) instead of the block size. K is a runtime knob, and the accuracy/latency trade-off it exposes is the main reason this is not simply a wider Markov head.

**Co-training.** The refiner is trained together with the drafter. Beyond the teacher-forced term, free-running Jacobi consistency rounds feed the refiner its own argmax and an anchor term holds the co-trained drafter's own logits to the target, so the Jacobi seed does not decay over a long run.

**Shared code, all opt-in.** The DFlash backbone can optionally return its anchor-validity mask behind a keyword argument, leaving the five-element return and every existing caller, subclass and test untouched. Two default-off DFlash config behaviours (an anchor cap and a prefix validity mask) and three general training options that are not XPress-specific: a separate validation corpus, one-conversation-per-batch batching, and a learning-rate scale for a warm-started backbone relative to a cold-started head. With defaults unchanged, no existing model's behaviour changes.

**Suggested order**, most general to most XPress-specific, rather than one large PR:

1. The three general training options above.
2. The opt-in DFlash backbone changes.
3. The XPress speculator itself, with unit tests in the style of the existing DSpark ones.


### Any Other Things.


**Results.** Qwen3-8B with a DFlash block-16 drafter, single-sequence decoding, at most 2048 generated tokens, one H200. `Sp.` is speedup over autoregressive decoding, tau is acceptance length. Each entry uses the throughput-optimal K for that setting. 

Temperature = 0:

| | GSM8K | MATH-500 | AIME25 | HumanEval | MBPP | LCB | MT-Bench | Avg. |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| DFlash tau | 6.48 | 7.71 | 7.10 | 6.44 | 5.75 | 7.11 | 3.18 | 6.25 |
| Markov head tau | 9.67 | 9.24 | 7.95 | 7.76 | 6.90 | 7.85 | 4.13 | 7.64 |
| **XPress tau** | **10.11** | **9.62** | **8.35** | **8.15** | **7.11** | **8.40** | **4.38** | **8.02** |
| XPress Sp. | 8.2x | 7.5x | 5.8x | 6.6x | 5.9x | 6.1x | 3.5x | 6.2x |
| Sp. over DFlash | 1.70x | 1.10x | 1.12x | 1.32x | 1.25x | 1.17x | 1.36x | 1.29x |

Temperature = 1 (lossless sampling, tau averaged over 5 seeds):

| | GSM8K | MATH-500 | AIME25 | HumanEval | MBPP | LCB | MT-Bench | Avg. |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| DFlash tau | 5.83 | 5.71 | 4.35 | 5.40 | 4.83 | 5.58 | 2.90 | 4.94 |
| Markov head tau | 8.76 | 7.60 | 6.22 | 6.99 | 6.39 | 6.43 | 3.97 | 6.62 |
| **XPress tau** | **9.20** | **8.12** | **6.68** | **7.36** | **6.68** | **6.65** | **4.13** | **6.97** |
| Sp. over DFlash | 1.60x | 1.58x | 1.48x | 1.46x | 1.51x | 1.23x | 1.39x | 1.46x |

**One design question we would rather settle first.** The refiner needs the backbone's anchor-validity mask, which `DFlashDraftModel._backbone_forward` computes but does not return. We currently expose it behind a keyword so nothing existing changes:

```python
def _backbone_forward(self, ..., return_anchor_valid: bool = False, **kwargs):
    ...
    if return_anchor_valid:
        return hidden, logits, targets, aligned_loss_mask, anchored_block_indices, anchor_valid
    return hidden, logits, targets, aligned_loss_mask, anchored_block_indices
```

The alternative is to have the backbone return a structured object instead of a bare tuple. That is cleaner, but it touches every caller and subclass, so we did not assume it. It does not change much of the diff, but it does change shared code DSpark depends on.

title: test_distributed_resume[ddp/fsdp] fails on any 2+ GPU machine: resumed scheduler lacks initial_lr in param_groups
body:
## Symptom

```
pytest "tests/unit/train/test_setup_model.py::test_distributed_resume"
...
KeyError: "param 'initial_lr' is not specified in param_groups[0] when resuming
scheduler with last_epoch >= 0."
```

Both parametrizations (`ddp`, `fsdp`) fail identically on unmodified `main` (reproduced at c05b95b). CI never sees this: the test is `@requires_multi_gpu` and the single-GPU runners skip it.

## Where

`Trainer.setup_optimizer` ([trainer.py#L342-L371](https://github.com/vllm-project/speculators/blob/main/src/speculators/train/trainer.py#L342-L371)): on resume it loads the optimizer state, then builds a fresh scheduler with `last_epoch=self.checkpointer.previous_epoch >= 0`. PyTorch's `LRScheduler.__init__` then requires `initial_lr` in every param group — which the distributed optimizer-state load does not restore, so the constructor raises.

## Environment

torch 2.11.0+cu130, 8x H20, python 3.12; found while validating #1029 (unrelated to that change — fails without it).

Happy to send a fix if useful — e.g. stamping `initial_lr` into the restored param groups before scheduler construction, or resuming the scheduler via its own `state_dict` (related to the exact-resume work in #1026/#1027).

title: [RFC]: Add native DeepSeek-V4-Flash DSpark support
body:
## Summary

This RFC proposes adding native DeepSeek-V4-Flash support to `speculators`: a DSpark draft built on DSV4's own architecture. The implementation and the training run are both complete. The target is `deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4-Flash` (Preview), not the later `DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731` release. The numbers below are measured against the released DeepSeek DSpark draft on the same serve (vLLM 0.23 + vllm-ascend, `num_speculative_tokens=5`, greedy, full `DATASET=all`):

| epoch | 0.5 | 1.0 | 1.5 | 2.0 | 2.5 | 3.0 | 3.5 | 4.0 | 4.5 | 5.0 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| mean accept_len | 3.84 | 4.06 | 4.18 | 4.25 | 4.29 | 4.35 | 4.36 | 4.39 | 4.41 | 4.40 |
| % of released (4.42) | 87.0 | 91.8 | 94.6 | 96.3 | 97.2 | 98.4 | 98.7 | 99.4 | 99.7 | 99.5 |

![current best vs released draft](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Sawyer117/speculators/feat/dsv4-dspark/docs/deployment/images/current_best_vs_released_final_ep5p0.png)

Per-dataset accept_len at the final checkpoint, on the same serve:

| | gsm8k | math500 | humaneval | mbpp | mt-bench |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| this draft, 5 epochs | 4.849 | 4.565 | 4.933 | 4.555 | 3.079 |
| released DSpark draft | 4.658 | 4.661 | 4.942 | 4.535 | 3.294 |

The curve is flat over the last three checkpoints: the five-dataset mean spans 0.014 across 4.0 / 4.5 /
5.0 epochs and gsm8k's per-checkpoint gain holds at +0.009. The learning rate is a cosine decay reaching
zero at 5 epochs, so the run ends fully annealed. Per-dataset and per-position numbers for all ten
checkpoints are in the evaluation ledger linked below.

## What is implemented

- A DSV4-native draft model: 3 × [MLA (q/o LoRA, per-head attention sink) + 256-routed/1-shared MoE
  (`sqrtsoftplus` scoring, `noaux_tc` top-k) + manifold-constrained hyper-connections], plus the
  DSpark Markov and confidence heads. It is registered as its own speculator type, not as a DFlash
  variant.
- Expert-parallel MoE training alongside FSDP2: each rank owns a disjoint slice of whole routed
  experts, and tokens reach their owner through an all-to-all dispatch (dropless), so the experts
  are held out of FSDP (`ignored_params`) rather than all-gathered. They are still exposed as
  `Shard(0)` DTensors on the same mesh as the FSDP-sharded parameters, so the optimizer, gradient
  clipping and checkpointing need no plain-tensor special casing. This part is model-agnostic.
- Warm-start controls: `--init-layer-from-target`, `--init-{moe,attn,hc,norm}-from-target` and
  `--init-moe-no-router`, initialising draft layers from chosen verifier layers.
- Opt-in `noaux_tc` load balancing for the draft router, following the DeepSeek-V3 rule.
- An online hidden-state path: a plain verifier serve produces hidden states that the trainer
  consumes as a rolling buffer, avoiding full-dataset materialisation.
- Conversion to the vLLM `mtp.*` serving layout, with an independent bit-exact check
  (2378/2378 tensors per checkpoint).

## Code

Branch: [`Sawyer117/speculators@feat/dsv4-dspark`](https://github.com/Sawyer117/speculators/tree/feat/dsv4-dspark).

Entry point:
[`docs/deployment/ascend-npu-dsv4-dspark-pipeline.md`](https://github.com/Sawyer117/speculators/blob/feat/dsv4-dspark/docs/deployment/ascend-npu-dsv4-dspark-pipeline.md).
It opens with a six-step reproduction path — environment, rollout, hidden states, training,
conversion, evaluation — with the exact commands, and indexes the per-stage design documents and the
evaluation ledger behind the table above.

Draft model:
[`src/speculators/models/dsv4_dspark/`](https://github.com/Sawyer117/speculators/tree/feat/dsv4-dspark/src/speculators/models/dsv4_dspark).

## Vendor-specific code

Development was on Ascend NPU (Atlas A2/A3, FSDP2 training; vLLM 0.23 + vllm-ascend for serving).
The vendor-specific parts are confined:

- The draft model is portable PyTorch. `core.py`, `config.py`, `weights.py` and
  `backbone/{attention,moe,hyper,rotary,norm,block}.py` contain no `torch_npu` import and no NPU
  call; NPU appears there only in comments explaining a portable formulation.
- `backbone/kernels.py` is a registry: each op has a torch reference, and a vendor bridge may
  register a faster implementation under the same key at import time. Nothing is NPU-only by
  default.
- Two modules import `torch_npu` — `backbone/moe_grouped_gemm.py` and `backbone/moe_compile.py` —
  with every call site gated on `device.type == "npu"`. They are throughput optimisations, not
  correctness requirements, and can be left out of an upstream PR or moved behind the registry.
- `examples/ascend_npu_dflash/` is operational tooling (launchers, serve scripts, analysis), not
  proposed as-is.
- The fork also carries small device-handling changes in the shared trainer; those would be
  rewritten against `torch.accelerator` rather than guarded `torch.cuda`.

A first upstream PR can therefore be device-agnostic, with the vendor bridge kept downstream.

## Open design question

The backbone is a clean-room implementation, validated component-by-component against
`transformers`' `deepseek_v4` — RMSNorm and the hyper-connection blocks bit-exact, MoE ~1.5e-7, sink
~1.2e-7 — with
[`dsv4_dspark_hf_parity.py`](https://github.com/Sawyer117/speculators/blob/feat/dsv4-dspark/examples/ascend_npu_dflash/dsv4_dspark_hf_parity.py);
routing and rotary conventions were cross-checked against torchtitan's DeepSeek-V4.

Three structures are possible: build on the `transformers` modules (less code, tracks the verifier's
implementation, but couples the draft to their layout), mirror an existing reference such as
torchtitan's, or keep a self-contained implementation. This choice determines most of the diff, so
we would rather settle it before writing the PR than assume.

## Proposed contribution order

Incremental rather than one large PR, from most general to most DSV4-specific:

1. Expert-parallel MoE training alongside FSDP2 (model-agnostic).
2. The `--init-*-from-target` warm-start controls.
3. `noaux_tc` load balancing for MoE draft routers.
4. The DSV4-native draft model.

Is upstreaming this of interest to the project, and if so, which of these components would you want
and in what order? Each can be submitted as a separate PR with tests, and the design can be revised
beforehand if any of it conflicts with planned work.

This work is by @zongzuo and me; questions and collaboration are welcome.

title: RFC: Ablation Study — Domino vs DSpark Performance Comparison
body:
## Motivation

Both Domino (#685, [arXiv:2605.29707](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.29707)) and DSpark add sequential/causal conditioning on top of the DFlash parallel draft backbone, but through fundamentally different mechanisms:

- **Domino**: GRU-based correction head producing additive logit deltas on suffix positions, with a dual-loss lambda curriculum that transitions from 100% backbone loss to 100% refined loss.
- **DSpark**: Low-rank factorized Markov logit-bias head (`W1 @ W2`, rank 256) + optional confidence head (per-position acceptance predictor trained with BCE).

Prior experiments have compared these methods, but never under identical conditions (same dataset, hyperparameters, verifier, and evaluation protocol). Weifan's DPace ablations (#736) and the v6 Domino experiments used different datasets and settings, making direct comparison unreliable. This RFC proposes a controlled ablation to resolve that.

Additionally, the v6 Domino experiments showed that the lambda curriculum improved the **backbone itself** by +9.1% MAL even when the GRU head was dropped at inference — meaning sequential conditioning during training can act as a regularizer that benefits the parallel backbone. Understanding whether DSpark's Markov head produces a similar backbone-strengthening effect is a key question.

**Inference support in vLLM:**
- **DSpark**: Fully supported in vLLM — `DSparkSpeculator` loads the Markov head and performs sequential left-to-right sampling with Markov bias at each step (`vllm/v1/worker/gpu/spec_decode/dspark/`).
- **Domino**: WIP/draft support in vLLM (vllm-project/vllm#48241), not yet merged. Pending testing with a training checkpoint.

**Note on parameter and compute overhead:** The Domino GRU head and DSpark Markov head add different amounts of parameters on top of the DFlash backbone. More importantly, they have different computational profiles: the GRU requires sequential state updates (inherently less parallelizable), while DSpark's factorized Markov bias is a single embedding lookup + matmul. Parameter counts and drafting latency will both be reported alongside quality metrics.

## Experimental Design

### Shared Configuration

```
--verifier-name-or-path  Qwen/Qwen3-8B
--num-layers             5
--target-layer-ids       1 9 17 25 34
--block-size             8
--max-anchors            3072
--draft-vocab-size       32000
--sliding-window         2048        # SWA default
--optimizer              muon        # Muon default
--lr 1e-4  --muon-lr 1e-3
--scheduler-type         cosine
--noise-std              0.0
--seed                   42
```

**Data:** 100K samples from Magpie+Ultrachat blend (same as the DPace ablations in #736 for direct comparability).

**Note on single seed:** All runs use seed 42. This means observed differences reflect point estimates, not statistically significant effects. Phase 2 (500K) provides a second data point at higher scale; multi-seed runs are deferred unless results are ambiguous.

### Phase 1: 100K Samples, 2 Epochs — Quick Signal

#### Core runs (must-do)

| Run | Type | Loss | Sequential Head | Inference | Key Extra Flags |
|-----|------|------|-----------------|-----------|-----------------| 
| A1 | **DFlash baseline** | CE | None | DFlash | — |
| A2 | **Domino** | CE | GRU | Domino (vllm-project/vllm#48241) | `--projector-type domino --domino-lambda-start 1.0 --domino-lambda-decay-ratio 1.0` |
| A3 | **DSpark (vanilla)** | CE | Low-rank Markov r=256 + confidence head | DSpark (Markov active) | `--speculator-type dspark --markov-head-type vanilla` |
| A4 | **DSpark (no confidence head)** | CE | Low-rank Markov r=256 only | DSpark (Markov active) | `--speculator-type dspark --no-enable-confidence-head` |
| A5 | **DSpark (confidence head only)** | CE | Confidence head only (no Markov) | DFlash | `--speculator-type dspark --markov-rank 0 --no-confidence-head-with-markov` |
| A6 | **DSpark as DFlash** | CE | Markov r=256 + confidence head (training only) | DFlash (Markov head dropped) | Same checkpoint as A3; eval as plain DFlash |

A5 isolates the confidence head's contribution without the Markov head (`--markov-rank 0`). If DSpark's gains are largely driven by the BCE-trained acceptance predictor rather than sequential logit corrections, A5 will show comparable quality to A3. The confidence head takes only `hidden_size` as input (no Markov embedding) when `--no-confidence-head-with-markov` is set.

A6 reuses A3's checkpoint but evaluates it as a plain DFlash model (ignoring the Markov head at inference). This gives a fair training-technique comparison: A1 vs A6 are both evaluated identically as DFlash, isolating the effect of Markov conditioning during training on the backbone itself. Meanwhile, A3 vs A6 isolates the Markov head's inference-time contribution.

**Lambda decay:** Domino uses a dual-loss curriculum `loss = (1-λ)*final_loss + λ*base_loss` where λ decays from 1→0. The current code uses absolute step counts (`--domino-lambda-decay-steps`), but for consistency across Phase 1 (100K) and Phase 2 (500K) we want ratio-based decay (like `--scheduler-warmup-ratio`). `--domino-lambda-decay-ratio 1.0` means λ reaches 0 at 100% of total training steps. **This requires a code change to the Domino branch** — the existing `lambda_base_decay_steps` will be supplemented with a `lambda_decay_ratio` option following the same pattern as `scheduler_warmup_ratio` in the trainer.

**Est.** ~20-25 hours on 8x H100 (2 GPUs for vLLM server, 6 for FSDP training). A6 reuses an existing checkpoint so adds no training time, only an extra eval pass.

#### Extension runs (lower priority, reference data exists at 1 epoch)

The DPace results in #736 already show DPace helps at 1 epoch on the same dataset (DFlash CE 2.485 -> DPace 2.617, DSpark CE 2.560 -> DPace 2.675). These runs confirm the effect at 2 epochs.

| Run | Type | Loss | Key Extra Flags |
|-----|------|------|-----------------| 
| A7 | DFlash + DPace | CE + DPace | `--per-position-loss-weight dpace --dpace-alpha 0.5` |
| A8 | DSpark + DPace | CE + DPace | `--speculator-type dspark --per-position-loss-weight dpace` |
| A9 | DSpark native | `{"ce":0.1,"tv":0.9}` | DSpark with its "native" compound loss |
| A10 | Domino native | KL (default) | `--projector-type domino --domino-lambda-start 1.0 --domino-lambda-decay-ratio 1.0 --loss-fn kl_div` |

A9 and A10 form a "best possible config" pair — each method with its empirically preferred loss — complementing the CE-controlled A1-A6 comparison.

#### Block size 16 follow-up

The Domino paper defaults to block_size=16. Larger blocks give the sequential heads (GRU / Markov) more positions to correct, which could disproportionately benefit Domino and DSpark over vanilla DFlash. After the core runs at block_size=8, re-run the top 2-3 methods at block_size=16 to measure the effect.

**Important:** If `--max-anchors` must be reduced for block_size=16 to fit in GPU memory, gradient accumulation steps must be adjusted to keep the effective token batch size (`max_anchors * block_size * grad_accum_steps`) identical to the A-series runs. Otherwise the comparison is confounded by different training dynamics, not just block size.

| Run | Type | Loss | Key Extra Flags |
|-----|------|------|-----------------| 
| B1 | DFlash baseline (bs=16) | CE | `--block-size 16` |
| B2 | Winner from A2-A4 (bs=16) | CE | `--block-size 16` + winner config |
| B3 | Runner-up from A2-A4 (bs=16) | CE | `--block-size 16` + runner-up config |

### Phase 2: 500K Samples, 5 Epochs — Confirmation

Run top 3-4 methods from Phase 1 at 500K scale with 5 epochs. `--domino-lambda-decay-ratio 1.0` scales automatically (ratio-based, no manual step adjustment needed).

### Evaluation Protocol

For each checkpoint:
1. Serve as speculative decoder via vLLM (using `DSparkSpeculator` for DSpark runs, `DFlashSpeculator` for DFlash runs, Domino inference path for A2)
2. Run `scripts/evaluate/evaluate.py` in **`sweep`** mode on all 9 `RedHatAI/speculator_benchmarks` subsets (sweep mode collects both acceptance rates and inference speed metrics)
3. Report per-subset and mean MAL (Mean Accepted Length)
4. Generate comparison plots via `scripts/evaluate/plot.py compare`

**Primary metric:** Mean MAL across all 9 subsets
**Tiebreaker:** Wall-clock output tokens/s — if two methods have similar MAL, the faster one wins. A +0.2 MAL gain that tanks ITL due to sequential head overhead (e.g., GRU state updates) is not a real improvement.
**Secondary metrics:**
- Inference speed: TTFT (time to first token), ITL (inter-token latency), output tokens/s — all collected by the `sweep` evaluation mode
- Drafting latency: per-draft-step latency (ms) to quantify the computational cost of each sequential head (GRU vs Markov vs none)
- Per-position acceptance rates
- Training-time EAL curves
- Training wall-clock time and peak GPU memory per run
- Parameter counts for each head configuration

## Open Questions for Discussion

### Q1: Loss function alignment

The core runs (A1-A6) all use CE for strict architectural isolation. Extension runs A9/A10 add a "best native config" comparison (compound CE+TV for DSpark, KL for Domino). Is this sufficient, or should we also cross the DPace dimension with native losses?

## References

- Domino paper: [arXiv:2605.29707](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.29707)
- DPace paper: [arXiv:2605.18810](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.18810)
- DFlare paper: [arXiv:2606.02091](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.02091)
- Domino PRs: https://github.com/vllm-project/speculators/pull/773 + https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/48241
- DPace PR: #736

title: [RFC]: Multi-node support
body:
### Motivation.

Scaling up speculators training can quickly hit limits of individual compute nodes. This is particularly an issue for online training workflows where some of the gpus have to be allocated to vllm hidden states generation, which can require multiple gpus for larger models.

For this reason, we'd like to be able to scale speculators training beyond a single compute node. This RFC explores the current blockers for this and implementation plan.

### Proposed Change.

## Stage 1: Offline multi-node datagen
Status: Complete
Implemented in #526. Simply shards the hidden states to generate between nodes, allowing them to be generated independently. Maintains data indices, so that hidden states can be combined.

## Stage 2: Offline multi-node training
Status: In-progress
Utilize `torchrun` / `FSDP`'s multi-node capability. To run training across multiple nodes. Currently requires all nodes to have the full preprocessed locally + access to all pre-generated hidden states. This is probably easiest enabled using some kind of shared network drive to store the generated hidden states.

Blockers:
- Some parts of the speculators library currently use `local_rank` instead of `rank`, which will need to be updated to handle the multi-node case.
- Needs testing

## Stage 3: Online multi-node training with co-located hidden states generation
e.g. Node 0 and 1, both w/ gpus 0-3 running vLLM, gpus 4-7 running training (training processes are synced across nodes, vllm processes are not)
Status: In-progress (should be possible whenever stage 2 is complete)

Blockers:
- Same as stage 2

## Stage 4: Online multi-node training with separate nodes for hidden states generation and training
This will be the biggest lift in training ability as it will allow a full node to be dedicated to hidden states extraction, will another node (or multiple) run the training loop.

The main challenge here is in getting the hidden states from the vLLM node to the training node. The current hidden states extraction system simply writes hidden states to disk where they can then be loaded by the training process. Technically this could be sufficient for stage 4 if using a shared network drive, but we'd like to have a better system.

That means we will need to implement a different HiddenStatesConnector based on either the Nccl, Nixl, or Mooncake KVConnectors. This will allow for direct transfer of the hidden states to the accelerator memory for the training process. This should help with performance for single node training as well.

Blockers:
- Better HiddenStatesConnector compatible with RDMA in vLLM

### Any Other Things.

_No response_

title: [RFC]: Add a staged layer-selection pathway for drafter training
body: ### Motivation Choosing *which* target hidden-state layers to feed a drafter is a decision that today is effectively a guess. In our Gemma-4-31B sweep the aux hidden-state layer id (or set of ids) had a meaningful effect on acceptance length — the best single layer beat the worst by a clear margin, and deep layers tended to beat shallow ones — yet we have no principled, cheap procedure for finding a good selection. We don't yet have enough evidence to claim how this ranks against other training decisions in general, but it is clearly a knob worth choosing deliberately rather than by default. Doing a full-data training run per candidate to find out does not scale: an exhaustive layer search at full data cost is prohibitive. *Acceptance length as a function of the aux hidden-state layer id, at both data scales. The choice of layer moves acceptance length substantially, and the shape of the curve is the same at small and large data — deep layers win at both.* The key empirical observation motivating this RFC: **a drafter's performance under a small amount of training data is highly correlated with its performance under a large amount of data.** If cheap runs rank candidates the same way expensive runs do, we can prune the search space cheaply and only spend full-data compute on the finalists. We measured this directly on Gemma-4-31B (`google/gemma-4-31B-it`), DFlash drafter, 1 epoch on ShareGPT, evaluated by drafts-weighted mean acceptance length across 9 held-out subsets, comparing **n=4096** (small) vs **n=65536** (16× larger) training samples per config. **Single aux layer, sweep of layers 0,4,…,56 (n=15 configs):** | Metric | Value | |---|---| | Spearman ρ (rank corr, 4096 vs 65536) | **0.914** (p=1.9e-06) | | Kendall τ | **0.790** (p=4.9e-06) | | Top-1 preserved across scales | 1 of 1 (layer 56 at both) | | Top-2 preserved across scales | 2 of 2 (52, 56) | | Top-3 preserved across scales | 3 of 3 (48, 52, 56) | *Each point is one single-layer selection; x = acceptance length trained on 4096 samples, y = trained on 65536 samples (16× more data). The cheap-run score reliably predicts the expensive-run score.* **Five random aux layers, configs sampled by depth category (n=12 configs):** | Metric | Value | |---|---| | Spearman ρ | **0.916** (p=2.8e-05) | | Kendall τ | **0.758** (p=2.4e-04) | | Top-1 preserved across scales | 0 of 1 (#-1 and #-2 swap order) | | Top-2 preserved across scales | 2 of 2 (same 2 configs) | | Top-3 preserved across scales | 2 of 3 | *Same relationship holds for five-layer selections: small-data acceptance length tracks large-data acceptance length.* The practical takeaway matters more than the aggregate correlation: **the top *set* is preserved even when exact order within it is not.** For single layers, the top-3 by small data are exactly the top-3 by large data (order included). For five-layer configs, the top-2 by small data are exactly the top-2 by large data as a set, but the #-1 and #-2 swap places — so small data does **not** reliably pick the single winner there; it reliably picks a small shortlist that contains it. This is precisely why the funnel carries a top-k (not top-1) from Stage 1 into Stage 2 to confirm, rather than trusting the cheap run's #-1 outright — while still spending ~16× less per Stage 1 run. ### Proposed Change. ### Proposed Change Add a **staged (funnel) layer-selection pathway** to speculators that turns layer selection into an explicit, cheap-to-expensive search instead of a guess. Three stages, each narrowing the candidate set while increasing the data spent per candidate: 1. **Stage 1 — broad search, small data.** Train many candidate layer selections on a small sample budget (e.g. ~4k samples, 1 epoch). Rank by acceptance length. Cheap enough to cover a wide search. 2. **Stage 2 — confirm, medium/large data.** Re-train only the top-k candidates from Stage 1 on a larger sample budget (e.g. ~64k). This filters out the small handful of cases where small-data ranking jitters, at a fraction of the cost of running everything at this scale. 3. **Stage 3 — final run, full data.** Train the single winning selection on the full dataset with production hyperparameters. Concretely, this would add to speculators: - A **selection-strategy config** describing the candidate space for Stage 1 (e.g. `single-layer-sweep`, `random-k`, `depth-biased` with late/uniform/early weightings — the sampling scheme we used here) plus `k` per stage and the sample budget per stage. - An **orchestration entry point** (script/CLI, e.g. `scripts/select_layers.py`) that runs the three stages: fan out Stage 1 trainings, rank by benchmarked acceptance length, carry the top-k into Stage 2, then emit the recommended selection (and optionally kick off Stage 3). - A small **results/leaderboard artifact** (CSV/JSON) recording each candidate's selection, stage, sample budget, and acceptance length, so the funnel is auditable and re-rankable. - Reuse of the existing `--target-layer-ids` training path and the benchmark harness — this is orchestration on top of what already exists, not a new training mode. #### Enabling infrastructure: runtime layer swap (depends on #996) Stage 1 runs *many* candidate layer selections back-to-back. Today each candidate requires relaunching the vLLM extraction server with a different `--target-layer-ids`, paying full model-load + startup cost per trial — which dominates wall-clock when each training run is itself cheap (small data). To make the sequential cheap experiments practical, we need to change *which* target hidden layers are captured **at runtime, without restarting the engine**. The draft PR **[vllm-project/speculators#996](https://github.com/vllm-project/speculators/pull/996)** (*"dynamic hidden-states layer swap for extract_hidden_states"*) provides exactly this. It adds an opt-in vLLM plugin that swaps the captured aux-layer *set* live over HTTP (`POST /aux_hidden_state_layers`) with no recompile and no `--enforce-eager`: it replaces the `torch.compile`-frozen `layer_idx in aux_layers` membership test with a masked accumulate over `N` fixed buffers, where the selection is a one-hot mask in a registered buffer, so a swap is an in-place `mask.copy_(...)` read live by both the compiled graph and captured CUDA graphs. This is the mechanism a Stage 1 orchestrator would drive: launch the extraction server once, then iterate candidates by POSTing new layer sets between trials. One constraint shapes the search design: **#996 fixes the layer *count* at launch (only the set is swappable).** So a single extraction server can sweep candidates of a fixed size `k` (e.g. all single-layer, or all 5-layer configs); sweeping a different `k` requires a fresh launch. This fits the funnel naturally — pick `k`, sweep sets of that size cheaply, confirm, commit — and is called out as a dependency/assumption for Stage 1 below. ### Any Other Things. #### Part of a broader hyper-parameter optimization suite Layer selection is the first concrete instance of a general pattern, and we propose building it so the machinery generalizes. The same cheap-predicts- expensive funnel — plus a shared candidate-config schema, staged orchestrator, benchmark harness, and leaderboard artifact — likely applies to many knobs in speculators training. #### Search within a fixed number of hidden states One design rule falls out of the data: **rank selections only against others with the same number of hidden states — do not pool across different counts.** The correlation figures above each hold *within* a fixed count, but the absolute acceptance-length scale shifts with the count, so a cross-count comparison is not apples-to-apples. *Both populations plotted together with separate fits. The five-layer cloud sits well above the single-layer cloud: at the same small-data acceptance length, a five-layer selection reaches ~0.2 higher acceptance length at large data. The extra hidden states add capacity, which shifts the whole curve — so a five-layer config and a single-layer config with identical small-data scores are not equivalent. The small-predicts-large property we rely on is a within-count statement.* This is why the funnel picks a number of hidden states `k` and searches sets of that size, and it dovetails with #996's fixed-count-per-launch constraint: a single extraction server sweeps one `k`, exactly the unit the ranking is valid over. ### Any Other Things Evidence appendix (full per-config numbers) and caveats: - **Data source.** Gemma-4-31B DFlash, ShareGPT, 1 epoch, drafts-weighted mean acceptance length over 9 subsets. Single-layer sweep = 15 configs complete; five-layer sweep = 12 of 15 planned configs complete at drafting time (will be refreshed to 15 before posting). - **Coverage caveats.** The single-layer sweep uses stride 4 and lands only on sliding-window (local) layers — it does not probe the 10 global-attention layers. Each (config, sample-size) point is a single run (1 epoch, one seed), so run-to-run variance is unmeasured; this is exactly why Stage 2 confirmation exists in the proposal rather than trusting Stage 1 outright. - **What "small data predicts large data" does and does not claim.** It reliably preserves the *top* of the ranking (what the funnel needs). It does not perfectly preserve mid-pack ordering — closely-scoring candidates reshuffle between scales — which is expected and handled by carrying a top-k (not top-1) into Stage 2. - **Generality.** Demonstrated on DFlash / Gemma here; the same funnel should apply to EAGLE3 / P-EAGLE and other targets. - **Dependency on #996 and its limits.** The efficient Stage 1 loop assumes the runtime layer-swap plugin from [#996](https://github.com/vllm-project/speculators/pull/996). Its constraints carry into the search: (a) the aux-layer *count* is fixed per server launch, so each server sweeps one fixed `k`; (b) live swap without `--enforce-eager` covers models that capture via `EagleModelMixin._maybe_add_hidden_state` (Qwen2/Qwen3, Llama, generic dense/MoE) — models that inline the membership test (e.g. `deepseek_v2`, `qwen3_next`) still need `--enforce-eager`, or a modified version of #996; (c) the extraction connector stores no layer-set metadata, so the orchestrator must record its own `{trial → layer set}` mapping. If #996 does not land, Stage 1 still works by relaunching the server per candidate — just more slowly. NB: I have more data for Qwen3-8B and Laguna-XS-2.1 with 1-layer and 2-layer that I will format and post below soon.

title: [RFC]: Checkpoint and restore RNG state so a resumed run reproduces the uninterrupted run
body:
### Motivation.

#603 restores the data position, optimizer and scheduler, but not torch RNG state. Anchor sampling, noise augmentation and dropout therefore diverge after resume, preventing step-by-step comparison with an uninterrupted run.

In our downstream trainer, restoring the torch CPU and per-rank accelerator generators made a fixed-batch resumed run match the uninterrupted run step for step. DataLoader worker RNG remains out of scope, so exact replay requires `--num-workers 0`.

### Proposed Change.

Store the torch CPU and current accelerator RNG state in one per-rank file alongside each resumable epoch checkpoint.

Capture mid-epoch state at checkpoint time and end-of-epoch state after validation and any best-checkpoint update. On resume, restore after creating the existing-epoch iterator for a mid-epoch checkpoint and before creating the next-epoch iterator at an epoch boundary. Checkpoints without RNG state continue with a warning.

Draft implementation: #1026.

This is necessary but not sufficient for bitwise resume; optimizer precision, scheduler position, model-weight precision and checkpoint completeness are separate concerns.

### Validation.

On a tiny CPU model with dropout and AdamW, a local branch combining #739, #899, #900 and #1026, plus full-precision resume weights, reproduced mid-epoch, end-of-epoch and `--save-best` resumes bitwise in loss, parameters and optimizer state. Removing scheduler position or full-precision model state caused immediate divergence, and the completeness marker must be published after the RNG snapshot.

### Any Other Things.

Re-seeding from `(seed, global_step)` cannot reproduce the uninterrupted generator stream when earlier steps consume a variable number of random values.

title: [RFC]: DFlash Training Best Practices — recommended configuration and reasoning
body:
## Motivation

We ran a series of DFlash training experiments on Qwen3-8B, covering vocabulary size, loss weighting, optimizer choice, anchor count, effective batch size, training data composition, and training schedule. This RFC proposes adopting the resulting configuration as a documented recommended default / best-practices reference for DFlash training in this repo, and surfaces the open questions we were not able to resolve, for visibility and discussion before finalizing anything.

If there's agreement on the substance, the concrete next step would be a PR adding this as a docs page (a draft already exists locally at `docs/user_guide/tutorials/dflash_training_best_practices.md`, linked from `getting_started.md` and `tutorials/index.md`) with the supporting charts included.

## Proposed Change

### Recommended configuration

| Setting | Recommendation |
|---|---|
| Architecture | DFlash draft model, `block_size=16`, 5 draft layers |
| Vocabulary | Full verifier vocabulary — omit the draft-vocab mapping (`--draft-vocab-size`) entirely |
| Loss | Cross-entropy + D-PACE per-position weighting (`--per-position-loss-weight dpace --dpace-alpha 0.5`) |
| Attention | Causal sliding-window attention (SWA), `--sliding-window 2048`, applied to all draft layers |
| Optimizer | Muon for 2D weight matrices (`--muon-lr` tuned per architecture, ≈3e-3 in our setup) + AdamW for norms/embeddings (`--lr` ≈6e-4) |
| Max anchors | As high as GPU memory allows for your architecture — see "Anchor count" below |
| Effective batch size | Large (hundreds of thousands of tokens/step) — see "Effective batch size" below |
| Data | A large, diverse instruction set with responses regenerated by a larger, same-model-family teacher, with targeted additions blended in from the start of training |
| Schedule | Run the full intended epoch budget as a single continuous job — see "Training schedule" below |

### Reference command

Configuration that produced our best result to date (4x H100, 80GB): full vocabulary, D-PACE, Muon, `max_anchors=1536`, 20 total epochs. Adjust `--max-anchors`, `--total-seq-len`, `--muon-lr`, and `--scheduler-total-steps` for different hardware/dataset sizes (see the relevant sections below before reusing as-is).

\`\`\`bash
torchrun --standalone --nproc-per-node 4 scripts/train.py \\
  --verifier-name-or-path Qwen/Qwen3-8B \\
  --data-path <path-to-prepared-data> \\
  --hidden-states-path <path-to-hidden-states> \\
  --vllm-endpoint http://localhost:<port>/v1 \\
  --save-path <checkpoint-output-dir> \\
  --speculator-type dflash \\
  --block-size 16 \\
  --num-layers 5 \\
  --target-layer-ids 2 10 18 26 34 \\
  --sliding-window 2048 \\
  --max-anchors 1536 \\
  --total-seq-len 65536 \\
  --epochs 20 \\
  --scheduler-type cosine \\
  --scheduler-total-steps <steps-per-epoch * 20> \\
  --loss-fn ce \\
  --per-position-loss-weight dpace \\
  --dpace-alpha 0.5 \\
  --optimizer muon \\
  --lr 6e-4 \\
  --muon-lr 3e-3 \\
  --muon-momentum 0.95 \\
  --muon-weight-decay 0.1 \\
  --muon-ns-steps 5 \\
  --muon-adjust-lr-fn match_rms_adamw \\
  --checkpoint-freq 0.1
\`\`\`

`--draft-vocab-size`, `--token-freq-path`, `--d2t-path`, and `--t2d-path` are intentionally omitted (see "Vocabulary" below).

### Vocabulary

The common EAGLE-style approach of shrinking the draft model's vocabulary (a `d2t`/`t2d` mapping down to, e.g., 32,000 tokens) simplifies per-token prediction, but reduces accuracy on rarer tokens and adds a mapping step. DFlash drafts an entire block of tokens in a single parallel forward pass rather than one token at a time, and is correspondingly less sensitive to vocabulary size than autoregressive drafters. In our tests, switching from a 32,000-token draft vocabulary to the full 151,936-token verifier vocabulary increased average acceptance length by approximately +0.3 tokens/round, with no additional inference cost.

### Loss weighting

DFlash's default loss applies a fixed exponential decay (`gamma`) to de-weight later positions in the block. D-PACE instead adapts the per-position weighting dynamically over training rather than fixing it in advance. Across every architecture variant tested (different anchor counts, different optimizers), D-PACE matched or exceeded the fixed-gamma baseline. We did not find a strong reason to move `--dpace-alpha` away from 0.5.

### Optimizer

Muon (2D weight matrices) + AdamW (norms, biases, embeddings, LM head) performed as well as or better than AdamW alone across every configuration tested.

**LR search methodology.** A short ablation on a small data subset can mislead: the LR schedule's warmup/decay shape has a significant effect, so `--scheduler-total-steps` in an ablation run should be pinned to the step count of the intended full production run. We identified `--muon-lr 3e-3` via a two-stage search (wide grid, then a narrower sweep around the best region) at our specific architecture (1,536 anchors, 65,536-token sequences).

**The `--lr`/`--muon-lr` coupling.** If `--muon-lr` is not passed explicitly, it defaults to `10 * --lr` (`scripts/train.py:1308-1309`). Sweeping `--lr` alone therefore sweeps both LRs together at a fixed 10:1 ratio — a reasonable one-dimensional simplification, but it never tests whether 10:1 is the correct *ratio*. We also noticed the effective resolved value isn't surfaced anywhere at runtime (not logged, not in `train_command.txt`), which made it hard to later confirm whether a given run's Muon LR had been independently tuned or was riding the default — worth a small follow-up fix regardless of the rest of this RFC.

### Anchor count

Higher `--max-anchors` consistently improved acceptance length in a controlled, single-variable ablation. The practical ceiling is determined by GPU memory and interacts with `--total-seq-len`:

| GPU | Max anchors | Sequence length |
|---|---|---|
| H100 (80GB) | 1,536 | 65,536 tokens |
| H200 | 2,048 | 147,456 tokens |

Exceeding this ceiling produces an OOM either immediately or partway through a full epoch once real batch-content variance is encountered (short ablation runs underestimate this). Leave headroom below the first observed OOM point.

**Open caveat.** A full training run at 2,048 anchors did not outperform a comparable run at 1,536 anchors on final acceptance length, despite the anchor-count ablation predicting the opposite — and this was not from a skipped LR search; the 2,048-anchor run's LR went through the same two-stage ablation process and converged cleanly. This is unresolved, not attributable to a known cause. Candidate explanations include the fixed 10:1 Muon:AdamW ratio above, or an anchor-count/architecture interaction not yet isolated.

### Effective batch size

Effective batch size (GPU count × sequence length, tokens/step) was substantially larger in our best configuration than typical LLM fine-tuning setups — ~262,144 tokens/step (4x H100, 65,536-token sequences). Two reasons to keep this large:

1. D-PACE applies a distinct per-position loss term at each of `block_size` positions, and `--max-anchors` samples many anchor positions per sequence; a larger effective batch aggregates more of these terms per gradient update, reducing gradient variance.
2. Muon's orthogonalization step is sensitive to gradient noise; larger batches produced more stable convergence in our runs, consistent with published Muon guidance.

### Training data

- Start from a broad instruction dataset with **responses regenerated by a larger teacher model from the same model family as the target** (we used Qwen3-8B as target, Qwen3-235B-A22B-Instruct-2507 as teacher), rather than the dataset's original responses or the target's own outputs. We did not directly test self-distillation or an unrelated-family teacher against this.
- When a specific weakness is identified in evaluation, source additional targeted prompts and **blend the fresh responses in from the start of training**, not only via a later-epoch extension. Blending from epoch 0 gave a consistent +0.1–0.15 avg acceptance length improvement in our tests.
- An FP8 teacher gave ~1.7x faster generation than BF16 with no detectable quality difference, given proper tensor-parallel sizing.

### Training schedule

More total epochs consistently improved results; we never observed a point where additional training clearly hurt. We repeatedly staged training in two phases (N epochs, evaluate, resume for N more with the schedule re-pinned) — every time, the first checkpoint after resuming showed a measurable regression before recovering, a re-annealing artifact rather than evidence the extension is unhelpful. No plateau was observed through 20 total epochs in our best run. **Recommendation: run the full intended epoch budget as a single continuous job** rather than staged resumes, to avoid the dip-and-recovery cycle.

### Results

Incremental application of this recipe on our internal benchmark suite (RedHatAI `speculator_benchmarks`, 9 categories, avg acceptance length):

| Configuration | Avg. acceptance length |
|---|---|
| Reduced (32k) vocabulary baseline | 3.425 |
| Full vocabulary, initial pass (prior to anchor/optimizer tuning) | 3.206 |
| + Muon, tuned anchor count | 3.612 |
| + targeted code/multilingual data, 20 epochs | 3.720 |
| Fresh restart on the same recipe and data, 20 epochs (current best) | **3.737** |

The improvement is consistent per-category and generalizes to GPQA Diamond, LiveCodeBench, and a separate suite (NVIDIA SPEED-Bench, 11 categories) — charts available in the linked docs draft.

## Any Other Things

Known, unresolved gaps rather than settled conclusions:

- **Code generation** is the most consistent weak spot across every benchmark tested, including two independent third-party code benchmarks. More/better code-specific data is the leading hypothesis, not yet confirmed.
- **Translation** performance lags other categories on our suite, though the absolute gap is small; a broader multilingual pass (not narrowly translation-focused) seems more promising than over-indexing on one benchmark's translation subset.
- Anchor-count ceilings were not cross-validated across GPU generations beyond H100/H200.
- **The anchor-count result above is unresolved, not merely under-tested.** Two full runs, each with an independently and properly ablated LR, still showed the lower-anchor configuration on top. A follow-up varying the Muon:AdamW LR ratio directly (not just their shared scale) at the higher anchor count seems like a reasonable next step before concluding more than "higher anchor counts helped in one isolated, single-variable test."
- Separately, we noticed `_resolve_scheduler_steps` (`src/speculators/train/trainer.py:128-138`) already auto-derives `scheduler_total_steps` from the real packed-batch count via `len(train_loader)`, which we were unaware of and never relied on — we manually recalibrated it from measured token counts on every run instead. If this default is reliable for online training with resumed checkpoints, it's worth documenting more prominently.
